title: Why Diwali Is Celebrated in So Many Countries
hook: What if Diwali had never left India? Without the people who carried it, many places far from India would have no Diwali of their own, including Fiji, Trinidad and Singapore.
era: Indian Ocean world and plantation colonies, 1800s
thumbnail_picture: Huge close-up on the right of a glowing clay oil lamp held in two cupped hands, a wooden sailing ship and dark ocean waves behind it, an Indian plantation worker in 1800s plain cotton clothes staring at the flame with wide, emotional, hopeful eyes, warm golden light against deep blue night, left third empty.

scenes.narration: What if Diwali never left India? Many faraway places, including Fiji, Trinidad and Singapore, would have no Diwali of their own.
scenes.caption: WHAT IF?
scenes.picture: Wide view of a small tropical island coast at night, palm trees and a sleeping village completely dark under a starry sky, one child standing on the beach looking at the darkness.

scenes.narration: But those places glow. Fiji, Trinidad, Singapore, Malaysia and Nepal all light up, and several give everyone the day off.
scenes.caption: GLOWING WORLD
scenes.picture: A tropical seaside town at dusk with rows of glowing clay lamps along walls and doorsteps, palm trees, warm orange light, happy families strolling.

scenes.narration: So how did one tiny clay lamp cross three oceans? The answer runs through monsoon winds, merchants, and ships.
scenes.caption: THE QUESTION
scenes.picture: A single small lit clay lamp resting on the rail of an old wooden sailing ship, rolling blue waves and a pink sunset behind it.

scenes.narration: To find out, follow the flame. It starts, as it always has, in a potter's hands.
scenes.caption: THE POTTER
scenes.picture: Close-up of an Indian village potter's hands shaping wet clay into a small lamp on a spinning wheel, dust and golden afternoon light, mud-brick wall behind.

scenes.narration: Wet clay, a cotton wick, a spoonful of oil. That's a diya, and it fits in your palm.
scenes.caption: THE DIYA
scenes.picture: Extreme close-up of an open palm holding a small lit clay lamp with a cotton wick, flame glowing, soft dark background.

scenes.narration: At home, hundreds line the windowsills and doorsteps, because light is how people say darkness won't win.
scenes.caption: LIGHT AT HOME
scenes.picture: A village house front at night with rows of lit clay lamps along the steps and windowsills, a mother and little child placing one more lamp, golden glow.

scenes.narration: But one thing deserves care: different communities tell different stories for this night, and each one is precious.
scenes.caption: MANY STORIES
scenes.picture: Four pairs of different hands, each gently placing a clay lamp on a long low wooden table, warm glow, shallow depth, no faces.

scenes.narration: Many Hindus in the north remember Prince Rama coming home to Ayodhya after years of exile, townspeople lighting his way.
scenes.caption: RAMA'S RETURN
scenes.era: Ancient India, as the tradition tells it
scenes.picture: A grand ancient Indian city gate at night, crowds of townspeople holding small lamps welcoming a prince on foot with a bow on his shoulder, his wife and brother beside him, golden light, joyful.

scenes.narration: In other regions, Hindus remember Krishna defeating the demon Narakasura, and many honour Lakshmi, goddess of good fortune.
scenes.caption: KRISHNA, LAKSHMI
scenes.picture: A family kneeling at a small home shrine with a golden statue of the young god Krishna beside a golden statue of the goddess Lakshmi seated on a lotus, among marigold garlands and lit lamps, warm evening glow.

scenes.narration: For Jains, it marks the night Mahavira reached liberation, and the lamps stand for the light of his knowledge.
scenes.caption: JAIN TRADITION
scenes.picture: A serene teacher in plain pale cloth seated under a tree at night, a few villagers sitting nearby with small glowing lamps, peaceful starry sky.

scenes.narration: Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas, remembering Guru Hargobind's release from a fort prison, with lamps glowing around the Golden Temple in Amritsar.
scenes.caption: SIKH TRADITION
scenes.picture: The golden-domed temple in Amritsar at night reflected in its still pool, thousands of tiny lamps glowing along the water's edge, deep blue sky.

scenes.narration: Newar communities in Nepal, Buddhist and Hindu alike, keep Swanti, their own version of the festival, with traditions all their own.
scenes.caption: NEWAR TRADITION
scenes.picture: An old brick courtyard in the Kathmandu valley with carved wooden windows, a woman in simple clothes placing small lamps on the ground at dusk.

scenes.narration: Different stories, one flame. So before it ever boarded a ship, this light already belonged to many hands.
scenes.caption: ONE FLAME
scenes.picture: Close-up of many different hands cupped around one single lit clay lamp, glowing warm gold, dark background.

scenes.narration: But a festival can't walk across an ocean by itself. Somebody has to carry it.
scenes.caption: WHO CARRIED IT?
scenes.picture: A lone traveller with a cloth bundle standing at the end of a wooden harbour dock at dusk, looking out at tall sailing ships at anchor.

scenes.narration: First came traders. The monsoon blows one way in summer and the other in winter, like a conveyor belt on the sea.
scenes.caption: MONSOON WINDS
scenes.era: Indian Ocean trade, ancient to medieval
scenes.picture: A wooden dhow with a big triangular sail racing across a bright blue sea under billowing monsoon clouds, spray at the bow.

scenes.narration: So merchants from India's coasts rode those winds for more than two thousand years, carrying cloth and spices to ports all around the ocean.
scenes.caption: SPICE AND CLOTH
scenes.era: Indian Ocean trade, ancient to medieval
scenes.picture: A busy tropical harbour with dhows moored, porters carrying bales of colourful cloth and sacks of spices, merchants bargaining in the sun.

scenes.narration: And merchants don't travel light. They pack their gods, their recipes, and their calendar.
scenes.caption: PACKED MEMORIES
scenes.era: Indian Ocean trade, ancient to medieval
scenes.picture: A merchant on a ship's deck carefully wrapping a small brass lamp in cloth and laying it in a wooden chest, ropes and sails behind him.

scenes.narration: So in new ports, they built little shrines. Diwali took firm root in Southeast Asia mainly in the 1800s, when later waves of migrants arrived.
scenes.caption: NEW PORTS
scenes.picture: A small modest shrine beside a palm-fringed harbour at dusk, a few merchants lighting clay lamps at its doorway, boats rocking behind.

scenes.narration: Closer to home, in the foothills of the Himalayas, Nepal made it a five-day festival called Tihar.
scenes.caption: NEPAL: TIHAR
scenes.picture: A line of pack mules and traders winding along a mountain path with snowy Himalayan peaks above and the green Kathmandu valley ahead.

scenes.narration: Nepalis honour crows, dogs, cows and oxen. Dogs and cows get garlands, and crows get treats. Even the animals get a party.
scenes.caption: ANIMALS GET A PARTY
scenes.picture: A friendly dog wearing a thick orange marigold garland sitting proudly in a Nepali courtyard while a child offers it food, lamps glowing around.

scenes.narration: Light had travelled by trade. But the biggest journey was not a choice at all.
scenes.caption: A DARKER TURN
scenes.picture: A huge dark sailing ship looming over a crowded harbour at twilight, heavy clouds, lanterns flickering on the dock.

scenes.narration: In 1833 Britain passed a law to abolish slavery across most of its empire, and by 1838 the system had ended in the Caribbean. But the sugar plantations still needed hands to cut cane.
scenes.caption: 1830s
scenes.picture: A vast sugar cane field under a hot sky with a grand plantation house in the distance, the fields strangely empty of workers.

scenes.narration: So recruiters walked into Indian villages. They promised steady wages and a ticket home. Many of those promises were bent or broken, and some recruits were tricked outright.
scenes.caption: THE PROMISE
scenes.picture: A recruiter in a long coat speaking to a small group of village men outside mud-walled houses, men listening with hopeful, uncertain faces.

scenes.narration: Many who listened were desperate, after famine, debt or failed harvests. A paying job overseas sounded like rescue.
scenes.caption: DESPERATE TIMES
scenes.picture: A thin farmer in a worn cotton dhoti kneeling in a cracked dry field holding an empty basket, worried face, hot pale sky.

scenes.narration: The deal was called indenture. Usually a contract of about five years on one estate. A free passage home came only after ten years.
scenes.caption: INDENTURE
scenes.picture: Close-up of a worker's hand pressing an inked thumb onto a blank sheet of paper on a wooden desk, a clerk's hand resting nearby.

scenes.narration: They gathered at depots in Calcutta and Madras: strangers from many villages and languages, all waiting for one ship.
scenes.caption: THE DEPOT
scenes.picture: A crowd of men, women and children sitting with bundles on a dusty quay, a big sailing ship waiting at anchor beyond them, early morning haze.

scenes.narration: Then the ship sailed. To Trinidad, the trip took around three to four months under sail, packed below deck with barely any room.
scenes.caption: MONTHS AT SEA
scenes.picture: Inside the lower deck of a sailing ship, rows of narrow wooden bunks, families huddled with bundles, one swaying lantern casting dim light.

scenes.narration: Many got sick on the way, and some never arrived. Those who did stepped off into a world with no familiar face.
scenes.caption: THE CROSSING
scenes.picture: A thin woman in a plain sari standing alone at a ship's rail at dawn, looking toward a distant green shoreline, tired and worried face.

scenes.narration: Back in the villages, families waited for letters that might never come.
scenes.caption: LEFT BEHIND
scenes.picture: An older woman standing in a village doorway at dusk looking down an empty dirt road, hands clasped, a lit lamp beside her.

scenes.narration: They owned almost nothing. But songs, prayers and recipes weigh nothing, so they carried those.
scenes.caption: LIGHT LUGGAGE
scenes.picture: Close-up of a small cloth bundle with a battered brass cooking pot and folded blanket lying on a wooden deck, sea glittering beyond.

scenes.narration: The first ship reached Trinidad in 1845. Over the next seventy years, more than 140,000 people followed.
scenes.caption: TRINIDAD, 1845
scenes.picture: A wooden sailing ship pulling into a Caribbean harbour with palm-covered green hills behind, small boats rowing out, bright morning light.

scenes.narration: Fiji's first ship arrived in 1879. In all, around 60,000 Indians made that Pacific crossing.
scenes.caption: FIJI, 1879
scenes.picture: A sailing ship nearing a turquoise coral reef beside a lush volcanic island in the Pacific, sunrise sky, gulls overhead.

scenes.narration: Then came the work. Cutting cane under a brutal sun, from before dawn, for wages that barely stretched.
scenes.caption: CANE FIELDS
scenes.picture: A line of workers in simple cotton clothes swinging long cane knives through tall sugar cane under a blazing low sun, sweat and dust.

scenes.narration: At night they slept in cramped barracks. It was hard, and lonely, a world away from every tradition they loved.
scenes.caption: THE BARRACKS
scenes.picture: A long row of plain wooden barrack rooms at dusk, tired workers sitting on the steps, one dim lantern, tall cane behind.

scenes.narration: But the seasons turned. Imagine one evening in October or November: a small clay pot, a little oil, a twist of cloth.
scenes.caption: A SPARK OF IDEA
scenes.picture: Close-up of a worker's rough hands making a lamp from a small clay pot, pouring oil and setting a twisted cloth wick, dim evening light.

scenes.narration: One flame, in a barracks yard, thousands of kilometres from home. For one night, the dark pulled back.
scenes.caption: ONE FLAME
scenes.picture: A barracks yard at night with a few workers and a child gathered around a single glowing lamp on the ground, faces lit gold, tears of joy.

scenes.narration: That's how Diwali crossed an ocean to stay: not on a royal ship, but in the memories of workers.
scenes.caption: THE ANSWER
scenes.picture: Wide dusk shot of a plantation yard where dozens of small lamps now flicker along the ground, workers and families sitting around them, smiling.

scenes.narration: Other workers went east. In Malaya, Indian labourers cleared forest for rubber estates and helped lay railways under British rule.
scenes.caption: MALAYA
scenes.picture: Labourers in cotton clothes clearing jungle beside rows of rubber trees and a half-built railway track with a steam locomotive waiting.

scenes.narration: In Singapore, a busy port, Indian traders, clerks and builders settled in neighbourhoods that still carry their mark.
scenes.caption: SINGAPORE
scenes.picture: A bustling street of colourful shophouses in old Singapore, a bullock cart, an Indian trader unrolling cloth outside his shop, busy crowds.

scenes.narration: Today, whole streets of Little India are strung with glowing lights for weeks before Deepavali.
scenes.caption: LITTLE INDIA
scenes.picture: A lively street at night under glowing arches of golden lights, families walking past brightly coloured shopfronts, festive and joyful.

scenes.narration: In Malaysia, Deepavali is a public holiday, and families hold open houses where neighbours of every background drop in for sweets.
scenes.caption: OPEN HOUSE
scenes.picture: A bright living room with a table full of colourful sweets and snacks, smiling guests of different backgrounds greeting a host at the open door.

scenes.narration: Now run the what-if again. Take away the traders, the monsoon sails, the plantation ships. What's left?
scenes.caption: THE WHAT-IF
scenes.picture: Tall sailing ships fading like ghosts into thick sea mist at dusk, only a faint glimmer of lamplight remaining on the water.

scenes.narration: Trinidad, where more than a third of people trace their roots to India, would be missing something huge.
scenes.caption: TRINIDAD TODAY
scenes.picture: A lively Trinidad street market in bright sunshine with palm trees, smiling vendors and shoppers, steaming food stalls, colourful awnings.

scenes.narration: Its famous doubles and roti wouldn't exist. Neither would the temples, or the songs drifting over cane fields.
scenes.caption: NO DOUBLES?
scenes.picture: Close-up of a street vendor's hands filling soft fried flatbread with golden curried chickpeas, steam rising, warm light.

scenes.narration: Fiji would lose its Diwali too, those evenings when rooftops flicker and neighbours swap sweets across fences.
scenes.caption: FIJI TODAY
scenes.picture: A Fijian village street at dusk with rooftops and verandas lined with tiny flickering lamps, coconut palms, neighbours passing plates over a fence.

scenes.narration: It would be a quieter planet: fewer festivals, fewer shared tables, fewer reasons to knock on a neighbour's door.
scenes.caption: A DARKER MAP
scenes.picture: A dim empty street at night with closed wooden doors and no lights in any window, one lone person walking away, cool blue tones.

scenes.narration: Here's the twist: the lamp survived because it didn't stay the same. It adapted wherever it landed.
scenes.caption: THE TWIST
scenes.picture: Three different lamps side by side: an old brass lamp, a simple clay lamp and a lamp in a bamboo holder, all lit, rich warm background.

scenes.narration: In Trinidad, families set hundreds of lamps along bamboo frames, and whole villages glitter like fallen constellations.
scenes.caption: BAMBOO LIGHTS
scenes.picture: A Caribbean village at night with tall bamboo frames dotted with hundreds of glowing clay lamps, people watching under a starry sky.

scenes.narration: In Nepal, it comes with flower garlands and rooftop lights. In Malaysia, with open doors. Same flame, local flavour.
scenes.caption: SAME FLAME
scenes.picture: A Kathmandu rooftop at dusk strung with marigold garlands and lit lamps, mountains in the background, a family smiling together.

scenes.narration: Today, strings of electric bulbs share the night with the old clay lamps, and nobody seems to mind.
scenes.caption: OLD MEETS NEW
scenes.picture: A city balcony at night where strings of electric fairy lights glow beside a row of small clay lamps, soft city lights beyond.

scenes.narration: So here's the answer to the what-if. Borders are young. Customs are old, and people carry them.
scenes.caption: THE POINT
scenes.picture: A grandmother handing a lit clay lamp to her young granddaughter in a doorway at dusk, both smiling, soft golden light.

scenes.narration: Recruiting stopped in 1917, and the last contracts were cancelled by 1920. The cane fields changed hands. But the lamps stayed.
scenes.caption: AFTER 1917
scenes.picture: An old empty plantation barrack with tall cane around it, a single lit clay lamp glowing on the wooden step at twilight.

scenes.narration: Their descendants became teachers, doctors, farmers, even national leaders, and every year at Diwali they light the way their ancestors did.
scenes.caption: GREAT-GRANDCHILDREN
scenes.picture: Four generations of one family on a veranda lighting lamps together at dusk, the youngest holding a taper, palm trees behind, warm glow.

scenes.narration: This year, Diwali falls on the eighth of November. Watch how the evening moves.
scenes.caption: 8 NOVEMBER 2026
scenes.picture: A huge orange sunset over a calm ocean horizon with a thin line of clouds, a silhouette of a lone palm on the shore.

scenes.narration: Dusk reaches Fiji first, then Singapore and Malaysia, then India, and finally Trinidad, hours later.
scenes.caption: DUSK TRAVELS
scenes.picture: A Pacific island village at the first moment of dusk, the first tiny lamps being lit along the shoreline, purple sky, calm lagoon.

scenes.narration: Lamp after lamp, a ribbon of light follows the sunset around the planet.
scenes.caption: RIBBON OF LIGHT
scenes.picture: Wide view from a hilltop over a sprawling coastal town at night with thousands of tiny glowing lamp lights spreading across rooftops to the sea.

scenes.narration: Behind every one of those tiny flames is someone who crossed a sea, and refused to let go of home.
scenes.caption: CARRIED HOME
scenes.picture: A silhouetted traveller on a ship's deck at sunset cupping a small lit lamp against the wind, calm sea and glowing orange sky.

scenes.narration: A flame needs very little to travel: a person who remembers, and a neighbour who stops to look.
scenes.caption: PASS IT ON
scenes.picture: Close-up of two neighbours on a doorstep at dusk, one lighting the other's clay lamp from her own, both smiling, warm glow.

description:
Why is Diwali celebrated in Fiji, Trinidad, Singapore, Malaysia and Nepal? Follow the festival of lights from India across the sea, carried by traders and by workers shipped overseas in the 1800s.
A what-if story about migration, monsoon trade, plantations and one small clay lamp. Hindu, Jain, Sikh and Newar communities each have their own stories for the day, and we tell them with respect. Diwali falls on 8 November 2026.

Sources and further reading:
- Hugh Tinker, "A New System of Slavery: The Export of Indian Labour Overseas, 1830-1920" (1974)
- Brij V. Lal, "Girmitiyas: The Origins of the Fiji Indians" (1983)
- Encyclopaedia Britannica, entries on Diwali and Tihar
- Singapore National Heritage Board and Indian Heritage Centre materials on Deepavali

Animation and narration are AI-assisted; script reviewed by a human.
